flawed_step: Step 2: inferring that X is independent of (Y,Z) from the two separate facts X ⟂ Y and X ⟂ Z. Separate independence does not imply independence from the joint pair.
counterexample: Let Y and Z be independent fair bits and define X=Y XOR Z. The four triples (X,Y,Z) are (0,0,0), (1,0,1), (1,1,0), and (0,1,1), each with probability 1/4. The (X,Y) distribution is uniform on {0,1}^2, so X ⟂ Y; likewise, (X,Z) is uniform, so X ⟂ Z. But P(X=0,Y=0,Z=0)=1/4, whereas P(X=0)P((Y,Z)=(0,0))=(1/2)(1/4)=1/8. Thus X is not independent of (Y,Z). Moreover, if S=Y+Z, then X=1 exactly when S=1, so X is not independent of Y+Z either; for example P(X=1,S=1)=1/2 but P(X=1)P(S=1)=1/4.
assessment_summary: Step 1 correctly records the two assumed marginal independence relations. The proof must stop at the next inference: those relations impose no sufficient constraint on the full joint distribution of (X,Y,Z). The explicit XOR construction satisfies both assumptions and contradicts both conclusions.
